title: How far below 0 °C does salt go?
hook: Road salt keeps water liquid below 0 °C. How far below for 58 g in a litre?

knows: that salt is spread on icy roads
that salt and sugar dissolve in water
doesNotKnow: that a mole is a fixed count of particles
that the freezing point falls with the number of dissolved particles, not their kind
that each unit of salt splits into two ions

misconception: Salt melts ice by heating it, or one mole of anything lowers the freezing point by the same amount.
objective: The learner can explain that 1.0 mol of NaCl in 1.0 kg of water makes 2.0 mol of ions, so the freezing point falls by about 3.7 °C (ideal), twice the 1.9 °C of 1.0 mol of sugar, because the drop depends on the count of particles.

claims.text: 58 g of table salt is about 1.0 mol of NaCl units, and 342 g of sugar (sucrose) is about 1.0 mol of molecules; 1 mol is about 6.0 × 10²³ units.
claims.source: Molar masses: NaCl 22.990 + 35.453 = 58.44 g/mol; sucrose C12H22O11 342.30 g/mol (IUPAC 2021 atomic weights). Avogadro constant 6.02214076e23 /mol (SI, exact).

claims.text: In water each NaCl unit splits into a sodium ion (Na⁺) and a chloride ion (Cl⁻); sugar molecules stay whole.
claims.source: NaCl is a strong electrolyte, fully dissociated in dilute solution; sucrose is a non-electrolyte (Atkins & Jones, Chemical Principles, ch. on solutions).

claims.text: In the ideal model, the freezing point of water falls by 1.86 °C for each mole of dissolved particles per kilogram of water, whatever the particles are.
claims.source: Colligative property ΔTf = i Kf m; Kf(water) = 1.86 K kg/mol (CRC Handbook, 'Cryoscopic constants': 1.853). Demo.tsx KF = 1.86.

claims.text: 1.0 mol of salt in 1.0 kg of water lowers the freezing point by about 3.7 °C in the ideal model, twice the 1.9 °C of 1.0 mol of sugar.
claims.source: 2 × 1.86 × 1.0 = 3.72 °C; 1 × 1.86 × 1.0 = 1.86 °C (node; Demo.tsx SALT_DROP, ONE_PARTICLE). Distractor 0.5 °C is arbitrary.

claims.text: Real salt water at this strength freezes a little less low, about 3.5 °C below zero, because the ions attract each other.
claims.source: Osmotic coefficient of 1 mol/kg NaCl about 0.93 (Robinson & Stokes, Electrolyte Solutions, appendix 8.10, 25 °C): 3.72 × 0.93 = 3.46 °C. Fact-checker: compare the CRC 'Concentrative properties of aqueous solutions' table for 5.5 wt% NaCl; if it gives about 3.3 °C, change 'about 3.5' to 'about 3.4'. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 5): left unverified. Ideal 3.72 x osmotic coefficient gives 3.4-3.46 depending on coefficient; measured freezing-point data for 1 mol/kg (5.5 wt%) NaCl interpolate to about 3.4 degC. CRC table could not be opened (no page fetch; searches returned only the ideal 3.72). Suggested fix: 'about 3.4 degC' (safe across 3.37-3.46), on the stage's muted line and in this claim.

claims.text: The stage is a toy: 1 dot stands for 0.1 mol of dissolved particles.
claims.source: Demo.tsx PER_DOT = 0.1: 10 sugar dots, 20 ion dots for salt. The stage labels it.

recall.question: Calcium chloride, CaCl₂, splits into one Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻ ions. Mole for mole, compared with table salt it lowers the freezing point…
options: more: three particles per unit instead of two
recall.why: Freezing point falls with the count of dissolved particles. CaCl₂ gives three per unit, NaCl two.
